learning.learning_goal: Understand no more than as an inclusive maximum and represent it with words, a number line, and a less-than-or-equal-to inequality.
learning.big_idea: No more than names the highest allowed value. The boundary counts, and every smaller value counts too.
novice_success_criteria: identify the maximum boundary from context
connect the closed point, leftward direction, and less-than-or-equal-to symbol

screens.label: Lesson 011 · Prototype
screens.title: What does “no more than” allow?
screens.body: Imagine a bag that can weigh no more than 50 pounds. Fifty pounds is allowed, and every lighter weight is allowed. Anything above 50 is not.
screens.callout: No inequality symbol is assumed. We will build the symbol from the maximum and the values it allows.

screens.label: Misconception
screens.title: Do not let the word “more” point you toward larger values.
screens.prompt: A room holds no more than 20 people. Which group is allowed?

choices.feedback: No more than includes the maximum itself, so exactly 20 people is allowed along with every smaller group.

hints: Ask whether the stated capacity itself is allowed.
No more than means the maximum or less, not greater than the maximum.

screens.label: Observe
screens.title: Build the allowed set from the maximum.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with a closed point at 50 and an arrow extending left toward smaller values
visual.caption: 50 is included; values smaller than 50 are included
visual.message: The closed point includes the maximum. The arrow shows every smaller value also works.

screens.label: Discover
screens.title: Which description matches the number line?

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with a closed point at 40 and an arrow extending left
visual.message: Start at 40, include it, and continue toward smaller values.

choices.feedback: The closed point includes 40, and the leftward arrow includes every value smaller than 40.

hints: Read the point first, then follow the arrow.
Leftward values are smaller on this number line.

screens.label: Language
screens.title: Name the maximum, boundary, and allowed values.

visual.ariaLabel: A number line with a closed point at 15 extending toward smaller values
visual.message: The boundary is 15. It is included, and smaller values are allowed.

screens.phraseMeaning: The boundary value is allowed, and so is every smaller value

definitions.meaning: the highest value that is allowed in the situation
a limit whose exact value is part of the allowed set
the boundary value or any value smaller than it

screens.guidance: Before choosing a symbol, test the exact boundary and one value on each side of it.

screens.label: Remember
screens.title: Maximum, included, then less.
screens.hook: No more than = the maximum counts, and less counts.
screens.body: Rebuild the inequality from what the situation allows instead of reacting to the word more.
rebuildSteps: Test the exact boundary; no more than includes it.
Mark a closed point because the boundary counts.
Extend toward smaller values, then choose ≤.
screens.boundary: This reconstruction applies to an inclusive maximum. Less than uses the same smaller direction but excludes the boundary and uses an open point with <.

screens.label: Symbol
screens.title: Choose the statement for “no more than 8.”

visual.ariaLabel: A number line including 8 and extending to smaller values
visual.message: Eight is allowed, and values to its left are allowed.

choices.feedback: The less side matches values below 8, and the line under the symbol includes 8 itself.

hints: The symbol needs both the smaller direction and equality.

screens.label: Reveal
screens.title: The symbol compresses the allowed set.

visual.ariaLabel: A closed point at 8 with an arrow toward smaller values
visual.message: Closed point = equal is allowed. Left arrow = smaller values are allowed.

screens.label: Guided practice
screens.title: Test values before choosing the inequality.
screens.prompt: A form accepts no more than 3 attachments. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: 3 and 2 are allowed, but 4 is not
choices.feedback: Three is the included maximum, two is smaller and allowed, while four exceeds the limit.

choices.text: 3 and 4 are allowed, but 2 is not

hints: Then test one value below and one above 3.

screens.label: Independent practice
screens.title: Reason without the model.
screens.prompt: A budget allows spending no more than $75. Which amount breaks the rule?

choices.feedback: Seventy-six dollars is above the included $75 maximum, so it is the only amount that breaks the rule.

screens.label: Recall
screens.title: Reconstruct the symbol from meaning.
screens.prompt: Why does “no more than 25” use ≤ rather than <?

choices.text: Because every value above 25 is allowed
Because the word more always means less
Because 25 itself is allowed, so equality must be included
choices.feedback: The line under ≤ records that the exact boundary value belongs to the solution set.

hints: The difference between ≤ and < is whether equality counts.

screens.label: Transfer
screens.title: Apply the boundary in a new setting.
screens.prompt: An elevator carries no more than 2,000 pounds. Which loads are allowed?

choices.feedback: The 2,000-pound boundary is included and 1,850 is below it; 2,001 exceeds the maximum.

hints: Test 2,000 before comparing the other loads.
Include the boundary and every smaller load.

screens.label: Reflect
screens.title: Which explanation shows understanding?
screens.prompt: Choose the statement that explains no more than.

choices.text: It excludes the named value and allows only smaller ones.
It names an included maximum and allows every smaller value.
It always points toward larger values because it contains more.

hints: Name the kind of boundary first.
Check whether the exact value is included.

screens.title: You built “no more than” from an inclusive maximum.
screens.body: You connected context, boundary testing, a closed point, smaller values, and the ≤ symbol.
screens.nextRecommendation: Contrast at least with no more than by testing the boundary before reading the arrow or symbol.
